title: Sam and Substrings
directAnswer: Given a numeric string, sum the integer values of all its substrings, modulo 1e9+7. The key is a positional DP: let dp[i] = the sum of all substrings that END at index i. A substring ending at i is some substring ending at i−1 shifted left one digit (×10) with digit[i] appended, plus the single-digit substring [i] itself. There are (i+1) substrings ending at i, so dp[i] = dp[i−1]·10 + (i+1)·digit[i]. The answer is the sum of dp[i] over all i. O(n) time, O(1) space.

remember.pattern: Positional 'sum of substrings ending here' DP (place-value contribution)
remember.formula:
MOD = 1e9+7
dp = 0          # sum of substrings ending at the previous index
total = 0
for i, ch in enumerate(s):
    d = int(ch)
    dp = (dp * 10 + (i + 1) * d) % MOD   # i+1 substrings end at i
    total = (total + dp) % MOD
return total
rules: Define dp[i] = sum of the numeric values of **all substrings ending at index i** — that's the state that makes the recurrence collapse.
Appending digit `d` at position i multiplies every substring ending at i−1 by **10** (place-value shift) and then adds `d` to each.
Exactly **(i+1)** substrings end at index i (starting at 0,1,…,i), so the appended digit contributes `(i+1)·d`, not just `d`.
The global answer is the **running sum of dp[i]**, not the final dp value — each dp[i] is only the substrings ending at i.
Apply the modulus to **both** the dp update and the total; the place-value ×10 makes values grow fast.
whenToUse: Sum/aggregate over all substrings or subarrays where each extends the previous by one element
Place-value or contribution-per-position reasoning turns O(n²) enumeration into O(n)
'Sum of all subarray X' problems (sums, ORs, numeric values) with an additive recurrence
Answer modulo a large prime over exponentially-valued substrings
antiSignals: You need the substrings themselves, not an aggregate → enumeration
The aggregate isn't decomposable per-position (e.g. distinct counts) → other techniques
Values fit easily and n is tiny → brute force is fine, DP overkill
remember.takeaway: Reframe 'sum over all substrings' as 'sum of substrings ending at each position', and a clean recurrence appears: each new digit shifts the previous bucket by ×10 and adds itself once per substring ending here. Contribution-per-position is the lever that turns quadratic enumeration into a single linear pass.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you find the per-position recurrence (dp[i] = dp[i−1]·10 + (i+1)·digit) instead of enumerating O(n²) substrings, and handle the modulus and place-value correctly.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Forgetting the (i+1) multiplier (treating the new digit as contributing once instead of once per substring ending at i), or returning the last dp instead of the running total.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Derive the recurrence from how substrings ending at i relate to those ending at i−1 (the ×10 place-value shift), then note it's O(n)/O(1) and modulo-safe.

problemStatement:
Given an integer represented as a **string** of digits, consider every **substring** of it as a number. Compute the **sum of all these substring values**, and return it **modulo 1e9 + 7**.

For example, for the string `"16"` the substrings are `"1"`, `"6"`, and `"16"`, i.e. the numbers 1, 6, and 16, summing to 23.
constraints: s consists of decimal digits (it may contain leading zeros in substrings)
The answer can be enormous → return it modulo 1 000 000 007
understanding: Every contiguous slice of the digit string is a number; we want them all added together. Listing all O(n²) substrings and parsing each is too slow for large inputs. The insight is to group substrings by where they end: when you move the right end one digit to the right, all the previously-ending substrings simply gain a digit on the right (their value times ten), and a brand-new single-digit substring appears. That gives a one-line update per position.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are substrings contiguous, or do you mean subsequences?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Contiguous substrings. 'Sub' here means a slice s[l..r]; subsequences would be a different (and harder) counting problem.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How should leading zeros be treated?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: A substring like "05" is just the number 5. Numerically, leading zeros vanish automatically when you build the value digit by digit, so no special handling is needed.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Why a modulus?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: For |s| up to 2·10⁵, substring values reach hundreds of thousands of digits and the sum is astronomically large. The problem asks for it modulo 1e9+7, so reduce as you go.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the ×10 place-value shift stay correct under the modulus?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — multiplication and addition are compatible with modular reduction, so reducing dp and total each step preserves the exact answer mod 1e9+7.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Enumerate Every Substring
approaches.whenToMention: State it to define the quantity precisely, then optimise once the O(n²) cost is clear.
hints: For every start index l, extend an end index r to the right, building the current number value = value·10 + digit[r] as you go.
Add each value to a running total, reducing modulo 1e9+7.
This visits all n(n+1)/2 substrings — fine for small n, too slow at 2·10⁵.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Two nested loops over start and end indices visit O(n²) substrings, with O(1) work each (the value is built incrementally) → O(n²) time.
approaches.explanation:
Enumerate every substring and add its value.

**The double loop.** Fix a start `l`. Sweep `r` from `l` to the end, maintaining the numeric value of `s[l..r]` incrementally: each step does `value = value·10 + digit[r]`, which is the value of the one-longer substring. Add `value` to the total at every step.

**Why incremental building matters.** If you re-parsed each substring from scratch you'd pay O(length) per substring → O(n³). Building `value` as you extend `r` keeps it O(1) per substring, so the brute force is O(n²), not O(n³).

**Why it's still too slow.** At `n = 2·10⁵`, `n²` is 4·10¹⁰ operations — far beyond a time limit. The fix is to notice we're recomputing closely related sums and to collapse the inner loop into a single recurrence per position.

**Modulus.** Reduce `value` and `total` each step so they never overflow.
approaches.insight: Even the O(n²) version already hints at the optimisation: for a fixed end r, all substrings ending at r share the place-value structure. Summing them in closed form per position removes the inner loop entirely.

approaches.name: Positional DP — Sum of Substrings Ending Here (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'group substrings by their right end and use a place-value recurrence'.
hints: Let dp = sum of values of all substrings ending at the current index. How does that relate to the sum for the previous index?
Adding digit d at index i takes every substring ending at i−1 and appends d (×10 then +d). The number of such substrings is i (their values are in dp[i−1]); plus the new single-digit substring d.
So dp[i] = dp[i−1]·10 + (i+1)·d, because there are i+1 substrings ending at i and each gains a +d. Accumulate dp[i] into the total.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single pass over n digits with O(1) work per digit → O(n) time. Only the rolling dp and total are kept → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Group substrings by their right endpoint and find how consecutive groups relate.

**The state.** Let `dp[i]` be the sum of the numeric values of all substrings that *end* at index `i`. There are exactly `i+1` such substrings: those starting at `0, 1, …, i`.

**The recurrence.** Compare substrings ending at `i` with those ending at `i−1`. Take any substring `s[l..i−1]` (there are `i` of them, summing to `dp[i−1]`). Appending digit `d = digit[i]` turns it into `s[l..i]`, whose value is `value(s[l..i−1])·10 + d`. Summing over all such `l`: the `·10` part contributes `dp[i−1]·10`, and the `+d` part contributes `d` once for each of those `i` substrings → `i·d`. Finally, the new single-character substring `s[i..i]` adds one more `d`. Total: `dp[i] = dp[i−1]·10 + i·d + d = dp[i−1]·10 + (i+1)·d`.

**Why the (i+1) factor.** It's the count of substrings ending at `i`. Each one acquires the digit `d` as its new last digit, contributing `d` apiece. Forgetting this and adding only a single `d` is the classic bug.

**The answer.** `dp[i]` is only the substrings ending at `i`. The total over *all* substrings is `Σ dp[i]`, so maintain a running `total += dp[i]`.

**Modulus.** Both the `·10` shift and the accumulation grow fast; reduce `dp` and `total` modulo 1e9+7 each step. Multiplication and addition commute with the modulus, so the reduced result equals the true sum mod 1e9+7.

**Space.** `dp[i]` depends only on `dp[i−1]`, so one scalar suffices — O(1) space.
approaches.insight: The whole trick is choosing the state 'sum of substrings ending at i'. Once framed that way, extending by one digit is a uniform place-value operation (×10) plus a count-weighted digit term — the quadratic enumeration telescopes into a single linear recurrence.

dryRun.intro: dp = sum of substrings ending at i = dp·10 + (i+1)·digit. total accumulates dp.

code.python:
def substrings(self, s: str) -> int:
    MOD = 1_000_000_007
    dp = 0
    total = 0
    for i, ch in enumerate(s):
        d = int(ch)
        dp = (dp * 10 + (i + 1) * d) % MOD
        total = (total + dp) % MOD
    return total

Shift prior substrings by ×10 and add d once per (i+1) substrings ending at i.

edgeCases.behavior: i=0: dp = 1·9 = 9; total = 9. Single digit returns itself.
dp 1 then 16; total 1 then 17? No: dp0=1 total=1; dp1=1·10+2·6=22 total=23 → 23.

pitfalls: Adding only a single d instead of (i+1)·d — undercounts the new digit's contribution.
Returning dp (last position only) instead of the running total.
Using int for (i+1)·d at large i — multiply in long before reducing.

commonMistakes: Omitting the (i+1) multiplier on the new digit's contribution.
Returning the final dp value instead of the accumulated total.
Skipping the modulus on the ×10 shift, overflowing for large strings.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the (i+1) factor
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The new digit becomes the last digit of all i+1 substrings ending at i, contributing d to each. Adding a single d undercounts.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: dp = (dp * 10 + d) % MOD          # only one copy of d
commonMistakesDetailed.good: dp = (dp * 10 + (i + 1) * d) % MOD  # one d per substring ending at i

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Returning dp instead of the total
commonMistakesDetailed.why: dp[i] is only the substrings ending at i. The answer is Σ dp[i]; returning the last dp drops every earlier position.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: return dp;          // only substrings ending at the last index
commonMistakesDetailed.good: return total;       // sum of dp[i] over all i

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Overflow on (i+1)·d
commonMistakesDetailed.why: For large i, (i+1)·d and dp·10 can exceed 32-bit. Multiply in 64-bit before reducing.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: dp = (dp * 10 + (i + 1) * d) % MOD;  // int (i+1)*d may overflow before promotion

patternNote: Contribution-per-position DP: reframe an aggregate over all substrings as a sum of 'aggregate of substrings ending at i', yielding a place-value recurrence dp[i] = dp[i−1]·10 + (i+1)·digit. The same 'best/sum ending here' framing powers Kadane's algorithm and Sum of Subarray Minimums — recognise it to turn O(n²) enumeration into O(n).
